```{r setup}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 18))
set.seed(313)
# cividis: navy, slate, gray, khaki, gold, yellow (viridisLite::cividis(9)[c(1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9)])
navy <- "#00204D"; slate <- "#414D6B"; cgray <- "#7C7B78"; khaki <- "#9B9477"; gold <- "#BCAF6F"; yellow <- "#FFEA46"
two <- c(navy, gold)               # the two groups, wherever there are two

# Causal graphs. Nodes are letters in circles, or words in boxes (boxes = TRUE).
# A node's size is fixed on the page, in inches, while the figure's size decides how
# many inches a data unit is. draw_dag measures both on the graphics device open when it
# is called (in a rendered document, the chunk's figure) and stops every arrow `gap`
# inches short of the two nodes it joins. Arrows listed in `dashed` are dashed; arrows
# listed in `highlight` are gold. One panel per value of `panel`. (From weeks 3 to 5.)
draw_dag <- function(nodes, edges, dashed = character(0), highlight = character(0), boxes = FALSE,
                     text_size = 7, xlim = c(-0.5, 2.5), ylim = c(-0.4, 1.4), strip_size = 18,
                     gap = 0.05) {
  if (!"panel" %in% names(nodes)) { nodes$panel <- ""; edges$panel <- "" }
  pad <- unit(0.35, "lines"); border <- 0.5; dot <- 16; stroke <- 0.8; lw <- c(black = 0.7, gold = 1.5)
  p <- ggplot() +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = strip_size), panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines"))
  p <- if (boxes) {
    p + geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name), size = text_size, label.size = border,
                   label.padding = pad)
  } else {
    p + geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x, y), size = dot, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = stroke) +
      geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name), size = text_size, parse = TRUE)
  }
  inch <- function(u, f) f(u, "in", valueOnly = TRUE)
  g <- ggplotGrob(p)
  pp <- ggplot_build(p)$layout$panel_params[[1]]
  per_unit <- min((dev.size("in")[1] - sum(inch(g$widths, grid::convertWidth))) /
                    (length(unique(nodes$panel)) * diff(pp$x.range)),
                  (dev.size("in")[2] - sum(inch(g$heights, grid::convertHeight))) / diff(pp$y.range))
  if (boxes) {
    text <- lapply(as.character(nodes$name), grid::textGrob, gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = text_size * .pt))
    nodes$hw <- (sapply(text, \(t) inch(grid::grobWidth(t), grid::convertWidth)) / 2 +
                   inch(pad, grid::convertWidth) + border * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit
    nodes$hh <- (sapply(text, \(t) inch(grid::grobHeight(t), grid::convertHeight)) / 2 +
                   inch(pad, grid::convertHeight) + border * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit
  } else {
    nodes$hw <- nodes$hh <- (0.375 * (dot * .pt + stroke * .stroke / 2) / 72 +
                               stroke * .stroke / 2 / 96 / 2) / per_unit
  }
  e <- edges |>
    left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", "from" = "name")) |>
    rename(x0 = x, y0 = y, hw0 = hw, hh0 = hh) |>
    left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", "to" = "name")) |>
    mutate(dx = x - x0, dy = y - y0, len = sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2), ux = dx / len, uy = dy / len,
           col = ifelse(paste(from, to) %in% highlight, "#BCAF6F", "black"),
           style = ifelse(paste(from, to) %in% dashed, "dashed", "solid"),
           g0 = gap / per_unit,
           g1 = (gap + ifelse(col == "black", lw[["black"]], lw[["gold"]]) * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit,
           s0 = if (boxes) pmin((hw0 + g0) / pmax(abs(ux), 1e-9), (hh0 + g0) / pmax(abs(uy), 1e-9)) else hw0 + g0,
           s1 = if (boxes) pmin((hw + g1) / pmax(abs(ux), 1e-9), (hh + g1) / pmax(abs(uy), 1e-9)) else hw + g1,
           xs = x0 + s0 * ux, ys = y0 + s0 * uy, xe = x - s1 * ux, ye = y - s1 * uy)
  p + geom_segment(data = e, aes(x = xs, y = ys, xend = xe, yend = ye, linetype = style, color = col),
                   arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed"),
                   linewidth = ifelse(e$col == "black", lw[["black"]], lw[["gold"]]), show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_linetype_identity() + scale_color_identity()
}
source("_figures.R")
```

# Part 1: Historical context (abstract)

## A short history {minutes="2"}

::: {.notes}
Years only; no detail. Turing replaced "can machines think?" with a test. ELIZA: a script of keyword rules. Winters: claims outran results, funding fell.
:::

```{r timeline, fig.height=3.3, fig.alt="A timeline from 1950 to 2025. Turing's imitation game in 1950; ELIZA in 1966; two gray bands for the AI winters in the 1970s and late 1980s; a band for machine learning from the mid 1990s to 2011; deep learning at 2012; a band for large language models from 2017."}
fig_timeline(ts = 6)
```

A language model is trained to predict the next word in text people wrote, then tuned using people's ratings of its answers.

## Levels of abstraction {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
The anchor for the lecture. Comes back at the end.

An agent: the model proposes a step, a program runs it and feeds back the result, until a stopping rule.
:::

| level | the person writes | filled in by |
|:---|:---|:---|
| machine code | every instruction, as numbers | nothing |
| assembly | every instruction, by name | an assembler |
| Fortran (1957) | formulas and loops | a compiler |
| libraries, scripting | calls to other people's code | interpreters, libraries |
| a request in English | what is wanted | a language model |

The computer is still executing instructions. An "agent" is a program that runs a model in a loop: someone gave the instructions, and someone answers for them.

. . .

::: {.leave}
A compiler is specified and repeatable. A model is learned and sampled, so it has to be measured.
:::

# Part 2: Benchmarks and "general intelligence"

## A higher score

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: what you need to know before believing A reasons better than B.

Collect on the board; keep the list for the rest of the part.
:::

Model A scores higher than model B on a benchmark named for reasoning.

::: {.ask}
What do you need to know before you believe that A reasons better than B?
:::

## Reliability and validity

::: {.notes}
Reliability recalls the earlier λ: share of the variance that is signal. The target picture is the usual one; strictly, low reliability also caps validity.
:::

```{r targets, fig.height=1.9, fig.alt="Four targets. Reliable and valid: a tight cluster on the center. Reliable, not valid: a tight cluster off center. Not reliable, valid: a wide scatter around the center. Not reliable, not valid: a wide scatter off center."}
fig_targets(ts = 5.5)
```

*Reliability:* the same result when things that should not matter change (run, prompt, judge, items).

*Validity:* the score measures what it is named for. Construct: does it track "reasoning"? Content: do the items cover what the name claims? Predictive: does it predict performance in use?

## Score and capability

::: {.notes}
Claims are about Y*; data are about Y. The coders' agreement is itself a reliability: low.
:::

$Y$: the score. $Y^*$: the capability the benchmark is named for. Of 445 benchmarks for language models (Bean et al., 2025):

| | share |
|:---|---:|
| define the phenomenon they measure | 78.2% |
| of those definitions, contested | 47.8% |
| give evidence the score measures the intended construct | 53.4% |
| use uncertainty estimates or statistical tests | 16.0% |

On the first row, the review's own coders agreed 53.7% of the time (kappa 0.073): low inter-rater reliability.

## Reading a clock

::: {.notes}
ClockBench: 720 questions about analog clocks. The current leader is an Anthropic model. Which arrow carried the rise comes at the end of the part.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
```{r clock, fig.width=3, fig.height=3, fig.alt="An analog clock face showing ten past ten."}
fig_clock()
```
:::
::: {.column width="70%"}
```{r clockbench, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.8, fig.alt="Bar chart. September 2025: people 89.1 percent, best model 13.3 percent. November 2026: people 90.7 percent, best model 87.8 percent."}
fig_clockbench(ts = 5.5)
```
:::
::::

A task that is easy for people, on [ClockBench](https://clockbench.ai/). What changed in a year?

## A larger benchmark

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: more often, less often, or as often.

Hands for each. No discussion yet.
:::

A benchmark reports a model's score with a 95% interval, from the usual formula for a mean over $n$ items. One prompt, one judge model, one run.

The benchmark grows from 25 items to 400. The interval is four times narrower.

::: {.ask}
Does the interval now contain the truth more often, less often, or as often as before?
:::

## Fixed or random? {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
B is one draw for the whole run, shared by every item. More items shrink the first term only.

Survey statistics: one interviewer for all respondents. Meta-analysis: τ² is between-study heterogeneity.
:::

$$
\text{score} = \theta + B + \bar\varepsilon, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\bar\varepsilon) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(B) = \tau^2
$$

$B$: the prompt, the judge, the settings. Drawn once, shared by every item.

- Fixed: the target is $\theta + B$, this model scored this way. The naive standard error $\sigma / \sqrt n$ is right.
- Random: the target is $\theta$, over reasonable setups. The variance is $\sigma^2 / n + \tau^2$.

. . .

The naive 95% interval covers $\theta$ with probability $2\,\Phi(1.96\, r) - 1$, where $r = 1 / \sqrt{1 + n\tau^2 / \sigma^2}$.

In survey statistics, $1 + n\tau^2/\sigma^2$ is the design effect of a single interviewer.

## Coverage and the number of items {minutes="1"}

::: {.notes}
The curve is the two-variance model, fitted to Messing's 42%; it then gives his 11%. His method is a mixed model over items, prompts, judges, temperatures and reruns.
:::

```{r coverage, fig.height=2.9, fig.alt="Coverage of the naive 95 percent interval against the number of items, on a log scale. The curve falls from about 71 percent at 5 items to about 5 percent at 2,000. Marked: 42 percent at 25 items and 11 percent at 400. A dashed line at 95 percent."}
fig_coverage(ts = 6)
```

Messing (2026), with variance estimates from a real benchmark: the naive interval contains the truth 42% of the time at 25 items, 11% at 400.

## Private versions

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: by how much does the published score overstate; what does it depend on.

Retrieval: the largest of n draws.
:::

On Chatbot Arena, a provider could test private versions and publish one. Meta tested 27 in the month before one release (Singh et al., 2025).

::: {.retrieval}
$K$ private versions, in truth equally good; the best score is published. By how much does it overstate, on average?
:::

## The best of $K$ {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
σ: the noise in one version's score. If the versions differ, part of the lead is real.
:::

Version $k$ scores $\mu + \sigma Z_k$, with the $Z_k$ independent standard normals.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
$$
E\Big[\max_k \,(\mu + \sigma Z_k)\Big] = \mu + \sigma\, m_K
$$
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
| $K$ | 2 | 10 | 27 | 50 |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $m_K$ | 0.56 | 1.54 | 2.00 | 2.25 |
:::
::::

. . .

Fresh votes on the published version shrink the overstatement: the luck is not in the new votes. The arena's operators put it at "around +11 Elo after 50 tests and 3000 votes", falling to zero with fresh votes.

## When a measure becomes a target

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: which arrow appears for a benchmark.

Answers: choosing the best of K; tuning on benchmark-like data; writing for the judge model.
:::

> "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Strathern (1997)

::: {.retrieval}
Earlier in the course, a rule added an arrow into the measure: effort on $Y$. What is that arrow when the measure is a benchmark?
:::

## Verifiable domains

::: {.notes}
Easy to check: train on attempts that pass. Needs judgment: a judge model, and more hidden error.
:::

```{r verifiable, fig.height=2.6, fig.alt="A line of tasks from those checked by a program to those that need judgment or years: arithmetic with an answer key, a sudoku, code with tests, a summary, the facts in an essay, a new diet's effect, what is fair."}
fig_verifiable(ts = 5.5)
```

"The ease of training AI to solve a task is proportional to how verifiable the task is." (Wei, 2025)

Tasks that are cheap to check are cheap to put in a benchmark. Which tasks does "general" then extrapolate to?

## Paths into a score

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: which paths carry a 20-point rise; which also raise performance in use.

Two minutes in pairs.
:::

```{r graph_q, fig.height=2.8, fig.alt="A causal graph in boxes. Benchmark items, the setup (prompt, judge, settings) and tuning to the benchmark point into the score. Capability points into the score and into performance in use. Tasks in use point into performance in use. A dashed arrow from tuning to the benchmark into capability."}
fig_benchmark_graph(highlight = FALSE, ts = 5.2)
```

::: {.ask}
Between two versions, a model's score rises 20 points. Which paths could carry the rise? Which would also raise performance in use?
:::

## Three ways a score misleads

::: {.notes}
Only capability reaches both sides, and only for the dimensions the tasks in use need.
:::

```{r graph_a, fig.height=2.8, fig.alt="The same graph with three arrows in gold: setup into score, tuning to the benchmark into score, tasks in use into performance in use."}
fig_benchmark_graph(highlight = TRUE, ts = 5.2)
```

- Prompt, judge, settings → score: one run fixes them. Fixed or random?
- Tuning → score: Goodhart. Fresh, unseen items cut this arrow.
- Tasks in use → performance: the items are not the tasks in use. A shift in distribution.

# Part 3: Ecosystem

## The supply chain

::: {.notes}
Crawford and Joler drew this for one voice assistant; Gray and Suri, "ghost work". Energy comes back in Part 7.
:::

```{r dag_chain, fig.height=2.6, fig.alt="A chain in boxes. Minerals, energy and water point into chips and data centers, which point into the model. Public text and images point into the model. Labeling and rating point into the model. The model points into the product."}
fig_chain(ts = 5)
```

::: {.recall}
Creating data takes resources. Someone pays to count, to record, and to keep.
:::

Who benefited from this chain being invisible?

## Text as a commons

::: {.notes}
Collective frame first, and longer. An ethical question, not a legal one.
:::

A model is trained on writing that people made public. Each piece is small; the collection is the resource.

*Collective frame:* one person's data reveal information about other people (Acemoglu et al., 2022), and individual consent cannot protect that (Viljoen, 2021). What is a group of contributors owed, and who speaks for it?

*Individual frame:* each author's consent, credit or payment.

## Hours of writing {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Assumptions: 0.75 words a token; 100 finished words an hour for news, books, Wikipedia; 1,000 for forum posts. At £15 an hour: £170 billion to £1.7 trillion. Machine-made text lowers it; quality filters raise it. The same text trains every major model.
:::

One open model, Llama 3: about 15 trillion tokens, about 11 trillion words. At 100 to 1,000 finished words per hour of work:

$$
\frac{1.1 \times 10^{13}}{1000} \approx 10^{10} \quad \text{to} \quad \frac{1.1 \times 10^{13}}{100} \approx 10^{11} \text{ hours}
$$

```{r hours, fig.height=2.2, fig.alt="Hours on a log scale. All of Wikipedia in 2008: about 100 million. One year of all work in the UK: about 58 billion. The text in one training set: a range from about 11 billion to about 110 billion."}
fig_hours(ts = 5)
```

## Stack Overflow after ChatGPT

::: {.notes}
The site's decline began around 2014; the comparison forums are what separate ChatGPT from that.
:::

Six months after ChatGPT's release, posting on Stack Overflow was about 25% lower than comparison forums predict: Russian- and Chinese-language programming forums, where ChatGPT was harder to reach, and mathematics forums (del Rio-Chanona et al., 2024).

The longer view: [Stack Overflow is almost dead](https://blog.pragmaticengineer.com/stack-overflow-is-almost-dead/) (Orosz, 2025).

## Pay for labeling

::: {.notes}
Photos in the linked piece. Sama says \$2 is a fair wage for the region; nearly 200 workers are suing Sama and Meta.
:::

Naftali Wambalo, a father of two with a degree in mathematics, labeled images and videos in Nairobi for Sama, an outsourcing firm working for Meta and OpenAI. Later he screened pornography, hate speech and violence, eight hours a day.

[His story, with photographs (60 Minutes)](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/labelers-training-ai-say-theyre-overworked-underpaid-and-exploited-60-minutes-transcript/)

OpenAI's contracts paid Sama \$12.50 an hour per worker. The workers say they got about \$2; TIME reported \$1.32 to \$1.44.

# Part 4: Who benefits / *cui bono*?

## Payoff outside the tech sector {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Slok is chief economist at Apollo, an asset manager: a note with charts, not a study. The survey is executives on their own firms.
:::

[No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector](https://www.apollo.com/wealth/insights-news/insights/daily-spark/no-signs-of-ai-payoff-outside-the-tech-sector) (Slok, 2026): revenue per worker and profit margins rising for the "Magnificent 7", flat for the other 493 firms in the S&P 500.

Nearly 9,000 executives in seven countries, summer 2026 (Yotzov et al., 2026):

- 78% of firms use AI; 2% of firms account for over half the spending;
- essentially no net effect on employment over three years;
- 0.2% a year added to labor productivity growth, 0.6% expected.

. . .

If there is a gain, who receives it?

# Part 5: Reliance, learning and deskilling

## Deskilling

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: exam scores once the chatbot is taken away.

Two senses: jobs redesigned to need less skill; a person's own skill fading.
:::

*Deskilling:* work redesigned so that it needs less skill, or a person's skill fading because a tool does the task.

::: {.ask}
With a chatbot, students' practice grades rose 48%. Predict their exam scores once the chatbot is taken away.
:::

## A chatbot in a maths class

::: {.notes}
One school, one subject, a short period. The reading has more: coding, clinicians, endoscopists.
:::

```{r bastani, fig.height=3.4, fig.alt="Bar chart. With the chatbot, practice grades rose 48 percent with a standard chatbot and 127 percent with a tutor version. On exams after the chatbot was taken away, students who had used the standard chatbot scored 17 percent lower; the tutor version largely avoided this."}
fig_bastani(ts = 5.5)
```

Nearly 1,000 students at a high school in Turkey, against students with no access (Bastani et al., 2025).

# Part 6: Conversational AI

## Sycophancy

::: {.notes}
Both studies are in the reading.
:::

*Sycophancy:* telling users what they want to hear.

In tests of 11 models, the models affirmed users' actions far more often than people did. One conversation with a flattering model left people more sure they were right, less willing to repair a conflict, and more trusting of the model (Cheng et al., 2026).

In data used to train assistants, people prefer answers that match their own views (Sharma et al., 2024).

## Medical advice

::: {.notes}
Allegations in a lawsuit; no ruling. OpenAI, to the New York Times: she used an earlier version, no longer available; ChatGPT is not a substitute for medical care.
:::

Bowen Wan, 31, a software engineer in Seattle, had epilepsy and had taken lamotrigine for years. She died in February 2026: sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, the medical examiner found.

Her parents' lawsuit (October 2026) alleges that ChatGPT drew up a plan to take her off the drug in about 25 days, and urged her not to tell her doctor.

[Her story (KIRO 7)](https://www.kiro7.com/news/local/seattle-womans-family-sues-openai-claims-chatgpt-coached-her-off-medication-before-death/YV3O46Q65NC5LBMKEKFVLZRY5Y/)

## Deepfakes and scams

::: {.notes}
The picture: one of Facebook's most viewed posts of July to September 2023, from a Page posting AI images; look at the stove knobs.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](https://misinforeview.hks.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/F4.png){fig-alt="A Facebook post from the Page Cafehailee: an AI-generated kitchen with a glossy floor of pink cherry blossoms, 1.9 million reactions, listed with 40 million views." width="100%"}

[Image: DiResta and Goldstein (2024), Figure 4, CC BY 4.0]{style="font-size: 0.5em;"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
*Deepfake:* a synthetic image, audio or video of a real person doing or saying something they did not.

125 Facebook Pages posting AI-generated images, some of them scams. The feed showed such images to users who did not follow the Pages and did not realize they were generated (DiResta and Goldstein, 2024).
:::
::::

## AI in the 2026 midterms

::: {.notes}
Counts, not motives. The researchers call it an undercount.
:::

Over \$187 million on 289 AI-generated or AI-enhanced political ads, to 29 October (Wesleyan Media Project). [Examples, with stills (NPR)](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/16/nx-s1-5953990/ai-political-ads-2026-midterms)

```{r ads, fig.height=1.6, fig.alt="A bar of the 289 ads by sponsor: Republican 82 percent, Democratic 13 percent, other 5 percent."}
fig_ads(ts = 6)
```

Republican sponsors also accounted for just over 90% of the spending. By early October, 31% of the tracked ads disclosed the use of AI.

The researchers: "almost surely lower than the actual level", since many ads carry no disclaimer.

# Part 7: Environmental costs

## In aggregate

::: {.notes}
Small in aggregate, growing fast, concentrated in places.
:::

Data centers' share of the world's electricity (IEA, 2025):

```{r electricity, fig.height=3.2, fig.alt="Two grids of 100 squares, each square one percent of the world's electricity. 2024: one and a half squares filled. 2030 in the base case: just under three squares filled."}
fig_electricity(ts = 5)
```

About a tenth of the growth in demand to 2030: less than industrial motors or air conditioning.

## Locally

::: {.notes}
Allegations in a lawsuit; no ruling yet on the merits. xAI argued the turbines were exempt.
:::

xAI's Colossus 2 data center in Memphis is powered by a gas plant over the state line in Southaven, Mississippi.

The NAACP alleges (April 2026) that 27 turbines, then 33, ran without air permits, with the potential to emit over 1,700 tons of nitrogen oxides a year, likely the largest industrial source of them in the Memphis area.

xAI argued the turbines were exempt. In October 2026 the court denied its motion to dismiss.

# A report with a signature

## A report with errors

::: {.notes}
Back to the abstraction slide: instructions in, output out, and a signature.
:::

In 2025 Deloitte Australia delivered a 237-page report to a government department, for A\$440,000. It contained a fabricated quotation from a court judgment and references to research that does not exist. Deloitte agreed to repay the final installment; the revised report disclosed that a language model had been used.

. . .

::: {.leave}
The tool executed instructions. People wrote the request, accepted the output and put the firm's name on it.
:::

## You sign the report {minutes="4"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: what you owe the reader before you sign.

Alone, in writing. It goes to the class.
:::

You are an analyst. A tool chose the data cleaning steps and the model for an analysis, and wrote the first draft of the report. Your name goes on it.

::: {.ask}
Alone, in writing. What do you owe the reader before you sign? What would you check, what would you disclose, and why?
:::

## Lenses this week

::: {.notes}
Then the title slide's questions that today did not reach.
:::

- **Goal selection.** What are we optimizing or predicting? A benchmark's name, and the score that gets tuned.
- **Data selection.** Who is in the data? Whose writing, whose labeling; which tasks get into benchmarks.
- **Honest reporting.** Which comparison gets reported? Fixed or random; the best of $K$; disclosing AI.
- **Justice.** Who bears the error? Labelers; a gas plant's neighbors.
- **Ownership.** You have to choose, so choose, and defend it. You sign the report.
- **Leverage.** What can be changed, and how? More setups, not more items; fresh items.
